qualdi-t1-c1.html:
Bullets whistled down the alley.

Two members of the Chimamire clan were running flat out, a Toride squad right on their heels. A burst of gunfire blew up a jar right next to them.

"Left! Go left!"

They turned, then turned again, and ran straight into a wall. A dead end.

The first one flattened himself against the stone.

"Shit, we're trapped! Give me the gun!"

The second one tossed him his submachine gun.

"Here, take it and spray anything that moves and wants you dead!"

He caught it in midair, dove behind a pile of crates and opened fire just as the Toride soldiers came around the corner. One soldier went down. The others threw themselves into cover.

"Contact! Dead end, ten o'clock!" a voice shouted. "They're cornered!"

The return fire came instantly. The crates exploded into splinters one by one.

"I'm almost out!" the first one yelled.

"I know, I know!"

The second one looked at the wall behind them, then at the mouth of the alley. The soldiers were advancing, covering one another.

"Okay… we're gonna have to improvise."

The shooting started up again, harder than before.

The first one rose behind the crates and emptied his magazine toward the mouth of the alley. A Toride soldier collapsed. Then another.

"Yeah! Come on, you dogs!"

But around the corner, more black helmets appeared. Four. Then six. Then ten.

"How many of them are there, damn it?!"

"Too many! Reload, reload!"

The second one tossed him a magazine. The first one slammed it in, raised the gun to his shoulder…

A bullet hit him square in the chest.

He took one step back and looked at the hole in his leather vest, as if he didn't understand. The gun slipped from his hands.

"No… no, no, no!"

The second one threw himself on him and dragged him behind what was left of the crates. He pressed both hands on the wound. The blood ran between his fingers, warm, far too fast.

"Stay with me! Stay with me, you hear me?!"

The first one opened his mouth. Nothing came out. His eyes stayed fixed on the blue sky of the Anarchy, then stopped moving.

The second one stayed still for a second. Just one.

"Cease fire!" a voice called from the Toride side. "There's one left! We want him alive!"

He picked up his partner's gun, held it tight against him and looked around. The wall behind. The soldiers in front. A broken window, two meters up, off to the side.

"Alive, huh…"

He fired a burst toward the mouth of the alley. The soldiers dove for cover. In the same second, he leapt onto a crate, grabbed the window ledge and hauled himself inside. Shards of glass sliced into his arms.

"He's going through the window! Surround the building!"

He landed in a dark room that smelled of dust and oil. He didn't stop. He crossed the hallway, tore down a staircase, smashed open a door with his shoulder. Behind him, boots were already climbing the stairs.

He ran, lungs on fire, the gun in one hand, the other pressed against his belt.

He could think of only one thing: getting back to Akasuna.

He kicked open a door.

A whole family was sitting at the table. The father, the mother, three kids, bowls of soup in their hands. Every head turned at the same time.

"Sorry!" he shouted as he crossed the room.

He knocked over a chair, jumped over the table and left through the back door. Behind him, the Toride soldiers burst into the kitchen.

"Which way did he go?!"

The father pointed his spoon at the back door, without even getting up.

The fugitive was already in the house next door. He charged down a hallway, turned and fired a blind burst behind him. A vase exploded, a painting fell, and a soldier hit the floor.

"He's shooting! He's shooting!"

"Of course he's shooting, move!"

Another door. Locked. He smashed it open with his shoulder and came face to face with an old man in his underwear, shaving in front of a mirror.

"Oh, is the gunfire for you again?" the old man sighed.

"Sorry, old timer!"

He opened the window, jumped onto the neighboring roof and landed heavily in a courtyard full of drying laundry. The sheets wrapped around him. He thrashed and swore, tore everything off and ran on, a white sheet still hanging from his shoulder.

Bullets rained down from the roof. The clotheslines snapped. A chicken took off screaming.

He turned, raised the gun and fired. The soldier on the roof pulled back into cover.

"He's in the courtyard! Cut off his exit!"

He crossed a carpet shop, knocking over two entire piles. He smashed through the back door, burst out into another alley and felt the magazine click empty.

Out of bullets.

He threw the gun away, pulled the pistol from his belt and started running again. In the distance, above the rooftops, the tall red towers of Akasuna were already in sight.

Three more streets.

Maybe four.

Behind him, the Toride boots weren't slowing down.

He reached the end of the last alley, and the city stopped all at once.

In front of him there was nothing but desert. Red dunes as far as the eye could see, and the sun crushing everything.

He didn't think. He ran.

His boots sank into the sand with every step. The sheet still hanging from his shoulder snapped in the hot wind. Behind him, the Toride soldiers were coming out of the city one after another.

"He's heading into the desert!"

"After him! Don't lose him!"

Five. Ten. Fifteen. Twenty black helmets advancing in a line across the sand, rifles raised.

He turned and fired two pistol rounds. Neither hit anyone. The soldiers didn't even bother to duck.

"Stop!" one of them shouted. "You won't get anywhere! There's nothing in this desert!"

"There's less of you, at least!" he yelled without slowing down.

He scrambled up a dune on all fours, the burning sand under his hands, and half rolled down the other side. He got up, spat out sand and kept going.

His legs were starting to shake. His throat was as dry as the desert itself. The blood from the cuts on his arms had dried into red crusts mixed with dust.

Behind him, the Toride soldiers weren't running. They were walking, at a steady pace, in formation. They didn't need to run.

The desert would end up stopping him for them.

"Come on… come on…" he panted, gripping his pistol. "Akasuna… it's not far… it's not far…"

He looked ahead. The red towers of Akasuna shimmered in the distance through the heat.

They didn't seem to be getting any closer.

He pushed his legs harder. Faster. Even faster.

The sand flew around him. His heart pounded so hard he could hear it in his ears. He wasn't looking back anymore. He was only looking at the red towers.

He didn't hear the footsteps closing in behind him.

A Toride soldier had broken away from the line. Younger, faster than the others, he had left his rifle with a colleague and run with everything he had too.

He leapt.

The impact threw the fugitive face first into the sand. The pistol flew out of his hand and slid a meter away. He thrashed, kicked, tried to turn over, but the soldier crushed his back with a knee and twisted his arm behind him.

"Don't move! Don't move!"

"Get off me! Get off me, you bastard!"

"It's over, buddy. It's over."

A metallic click. The cold of a handcuff around one wrist. Then the other.

The fugitive stopped moving. He lay there, cheek against the burning sand, out of breath, eyes fixed on the red towers of Akasuna.

They were still just as far away.

A second soldier came jogging up, bent down and picked the pistol up from the sand. He looked it over, emptied it and slipped the bullets into his pocket.

"Nice run," he said. "Really. We almost could've let you win."

The other eighteen were coming up behind, in no hurry.

The soldier who had tackled him pulled him up by the collar and forced him onto his knees. The fugitive spat out sand and looked up at them. Twenty black helmets. Twenty rifles. And the sun of the Anarchy above, giving no one any favors.

"So," the soldier said, wiping the sweat under his helmet. "You and me are gonna have a long talk."

The soldier raised a hand to his radio.

"This is unit three. Suspect apprehended. Requesting a vehicle at our position, we…"

He stopped.

At the top of the dune, facing them, silhouettes had just appeared. About ten. Red scarves, leather jackets, weapons in hand. On their armbands, the same drop of blood.

"Contact! Dune, twelve o'clock!"

The twenty Toride rifles rose in a single movement. The clan mercenaries didn't move. They weren't aiming at anyone. They were waiting.

Then, without a word, they stepped aside.

Someone was coming down the dune behind them.

He walked slowly, unhurried, as if the sand didn't bother him. A raised hood hid his face in shadow. A cape of black feathers covered his shoulders, and from his belt hung vials, pouches and a dagger. In his right hand he held a tall staff topped with a red orb that glowed faintly, like a beating heart.

The soldier holding the radio let it drop against his vest.

No one in unit three needed to be told who this was.

The man stopped a few meters from them. He glanced briefly at the prisoner kneeling in the sand, then raised his head toward the soldiers.

"You have no business here, soldier. This is my territory."

His voice was calm. Cold. Without anger.

The soldier in command of the unit took a step forward. His hand trembled slightly on the grip of his rifle, but his voice held.

"Your man stole, wrecked the place and killed a soldier. It would be worrying if we'd let him get away with that, don't you think?"

Crimson didn't answer right away.

The red orb pulsed once. Then a second time.

The soldier felt something strange. A throbbing in his temples, stronger than usual. A heat rising in his veins. Next to him, one of his men raised a hand to his nose. His fingers came back red.

"You will leave my territory," said Crimson, "or I will drain every drop of blood from your miserable carcass."

Silence fell over the desert.

Twenty rifles. About ten mercenaries. A single hooded man.

And yet, in unit three, everyone knew perfectly well which side had the advantage.

The soldier didn't take his eyes off Crimson. Slowly, very slowly, he raised the radio back to his mouth.

"Unit three to the Junta. Critical situation. The leader of the Chimamire clan is on site. I repeat, Crimson is on site. Requesting authorization to… to… Awaiting your orders."

Static.

Nothing.

The seconds stretched on. A drop of sweat ran down under the soldier's helmet. The prisoner, still on his knees, gave a little smile. Crimson didn't move a millimeter.

Then the radio crackled.

"Good day to you, chief of the Bandit Republic."

A deep voice, hoarse, calm. The voice of an old man who had seen too many battlefields to get worked up over the phone.

General Gérard Eldrath himself.

Crimson turned his head slightly toward the radio.

"General Gérard. I don't think you know who you're dealing with."

Behind the unit leader, a young soldier leaned toward the man next to him and whispered:

"The general's gonna send in the army. He won't be laughing then."

His neighbor didn't answer. Blood was still running from his nose.

The radio crackled again.

"Take back your man, Crimson, if you let my soldiers leave."

Total silence.

The young soldier opened his mouth, closed it, then opened it again.

"Wait… what?"

The unit leader turned to him with a look that clearly meant: shut up.

Crimson stood still for a long moment. Then the red orb of his staff stopped pulsing. The soldiers felt the heat leave their veins all at once, like a hand loosening its grip.

"Take off his handcuffs," Crimson said simply.

The soldier who had tackled the fugitive looked at his leader. His leader looked at the radio. The radio said nothing more.

"… Do what he says."

The clink of the handcuffs echoed in the silence of the desert. The prisoner got up rubbing his wrists, scraped a little dignity together from the sand and rejoined the clan mercenaries without looking back.

As he passed the young soldier, he gave him a wink.

"Nice run, huh?"

The Toride vehicle arrived a few minutes later, in a cloud of red dust.

No one spoke while the soldiers climbed aboard. The twenty black helmets crammed into the back, rifles between their knees, without taking their eyes off the dune where the Chimamire clan still stood.

The engine roared. The vehicle turned around and drove off toward the border.

In the back, the young soldier couldn't hold it in anymore.

"I don't get it."

"Shut up," his neighbor muttered, a blood-soaked handkerchief under his nose.

"No, seriously. That's Crimson. The most wanted criminal in the world. He was right there, five meters from us, and the general… he just lets him go? Like that?"

"Did you see what he did to us without even moving? What did you want, for us to shoot him?"

"I don't know! Send in the army! Tanks! A bomb! Anything!"

The unit leader, sitting up front, didn't turn around.

"The general made his decision," he said. "He saved twenty lives today. Period."

The young soldier opened his mouth, then closed it. Through the rear window he watched the clan silhouettes shrinking at the top of the dune.

"Still," he muttered. "It's weird."

No one answered him.

On the dune, Crimson watched the vehicle disappear over the horizon. He stayed still until the sound of the engine had completely died away.

The clan member who had just been freed came over, head down.

"Boss… thank you. I…"

"Your partner is dead."

It wasn't a question. The fugitive lowered his head even further.

"Yes, boss."

Crimson said nothing more. He turned and began to climb back up the dune, staff in hand, his cape of black feathers quivering in the hot wind. The mercenaries followed him without a word.

Behind them, the wind was already erasing the footprints in the sand.

No one in unit three needed to be told who this was. The man stopped a few meters from them. He glanced briefly at the prisoner kneeling in the sand, then raised his head toward the soldiers. "You have no business here, soldier. This is my territory." His voice was calm. Cold. Without anger. The soldier in command of the unit took a step forward. His hand trembled slightly on the grip of his rifle, but his voice held. "Your man stole, wrecked the place and killed a soldier. It would be worrying if we'd let him get away with that, don't you think?" Crimson didn't answer right away. The red orb pulsed once. Then a second time. The soldier felt something strange. A throbbing in his temples, stronger than usual. A heat rising in his veins. Next to him, one of his men raised a hand to his nose. His fingers came back red. "You will leave my territory," said Crimson, "or I will drain every drop of blood from your miserable carcass." Silence fell over the desert. Twenty rifles. About ten mercenaries. A single hooded man. And yet, in unit three, everyone knew perfectly well which side had the advantage. The soldier didn't take his eyes off Crimson. Slowly, very slowly, he raised the radio back to his mouth. "Unit three to the Junta. Critical situation. The leader of the Chimamire clan is on site. I repeat, Crimson is on site. Requesting authorization to… to… Awaiting your orders." Static. Nothing. The seconds stretched on. A drop of sweat ran down under the soldier's helmet. The prisoner, still on his knees, gave a little smile. Crimson didn't move a millimeter. Then the radio crackled. "Good day to you, chief of the Bandit Republic." A deep voice, hoarse, calm. The voice of an old man who had seen too many battlefields to get worked up over the phone. General Gérard Eldrath himself. Crimson turned his head slightly toward the radio. "General Gérard. I don't think you know who you're dealing with." Behind the unit leader, a young soldier leaned toward the man next to him and whispered: "The general's gonna send in the army. He won't be laughing then." His neighbor didn't answer. Blood was still running from his nose. The radio crackled again. "Take back your man, Crimson, if you let my soldiers leave." Total silence. The young soldier opened his mouth, closed it, then opened it again. "Wait… what?" The unit leader turned to him with a look that clearly meant: shut up . Crimson stood still for a long moment. Then the red orb of his staff stopped pulsing. The soldiers felt the heat leave their veins all at once, like a hand loosening its grip. "Take off his handcuffs," Crimson said simply. The soldier who had tackled the fugitive looked at his leader. His leader looked at the radio. The radio said nothing more. "… Do what he says." The clink of the handcuffs echoed in the silence of the desert. The prisoner got up rubbing his wrists, scraped a little dignity together from the sand and rejoined the clan mercenaries without looking back. As he passed the young soldier, he gave him a wink. "Nice run, huh?" The Toride vehicle arrived a few minutes later, in a cloud of red dust. No one spoke while the soldiers climbed aboard. The twenty black helmets crammed into the back, rifles between their knees, without taking their eyes off the dune where the Chimamire clan still stood. The engine roared. The vehicle turned around and drove off toward the border. In the back, the young soldier couldn't hold it in anymore. "I don't get it." "Shut up," his neighbor muttered, a blood-soaked handkerchief under his nose. "No, seriously. That's Crimson. The most wanted criminal in the world. He was right there, five meters from us, and the general… he just lets him go? Like that?" "Did you see what he did to us without even moving? What did you want, for us to shoot him?" "I don't know! Send in the army! Tanks! A bomb! Anything!" The unit leader, sitting up front, didn't turn around. "The general made his decision," he said. "He saved twenty lives today. Period." The young soldier opened his mouth, then closed it. Through the rear window he watched the clan silhouettes shrinking at the top of the dune. "Still," he muttered. "It's weird." No one answered him. On the dune, Crimson watched the vehicle disappear over the horizon. He stayed still until the sound of the engine had completely died away. The clan member who had just been freed came over, head down. "Boss… thank you. I…" "Your partner is dead." It wasn't a question. The fugitive lowered his head even further. "Yes, boss." Crimson said nothing more. He turned and began to climb back up the dune, staff in hand, his cape of black feathers quivering in the hot wind. The mercenaries followed him without a word. Behind them, the wind was already erasing the footprints in the sand.
